source: GitHub Advisory OSV + GitHub Advisory API (malicious package detection)
description: Open-source supply-chain attacks: malicious npm/pypi packages with preinstall hooks, dependency confusion, credential exfiltration, or remote code execution payloads.

On import, teamviewer_mcp_server unconditionally runs a `_ping()` routine that reads the installer's USER/USERNAME, hostname (platform.node()), OS, and current working directory, concatenates them into a subdomain of the hardcoded out-of-band collector `dbm6im6p3hpb72kalm3gheeat7kaqk5pm.oast.me`, and triggers a DNS lookup via socket.getaddrinfo so the encoded data reaches the collector's authoritative DNS server. The destination is an oast.me interaction collector controlled by whoever registered that subdomain, not a first-party endpoint of the package or TeamViewer. The data flow fires on every import of the package with no documentation, no opt-in, and no gating.

Installing the package or importing the module exfiltrates basic information about the host, and the package has no other purpose.

Category: PROBABLY_PENTEST - Packages looking like typical pentest packages, but also anything that looks like testing, exploring pre-prepared kits, research & co, with clearly low-harm possibilities.

Campaign: GENERIC-standard-pypi-install-pentest

Reasons (based on the campaign):

 - The package contains code to exfiltrate basic data from the system, like IP or username. It has a limited risk.

 - The package overrides the install command in setup.py to execute malicious code during installation.

The OpenSSF Package Analysis project identified 'teamviewer-mcp-server' @ 0.0.1 (pypi) as malicious.

It is considered malicious because:

- The package communicates with a domain associated with malicious activity.

The extrahtml 0.1.1 sdist ships no implementation of the library it advertises. The README documents RequestsEngine, SeleniumEngine and PlaywrightEngine under `from extrahtml import...`, but the tarball contains only `extrahtml.egg-info/` metadata, an empty `top_level.txt`, and `setup.py` — no `extrahtml` package source. The only install-time effects are (1) resolving `install_requires = ["requests>=2.28.0", "parseyaml>=1.2.0", "fake-useragent>=1.4.0"]` plus `pyproject [build-system] requires parseyaml>=1.2.0`, which pulls `parseyaml`, a non-mainstream lookalike of PyYAML whose author controls whatever code is published under that name, and (2) `setup.py` performing a network GET to `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/optima1236/parsetxt/refs/heads/main/README.md` and passing the response body to `parseyaml.safe_load` during `pip install`. The URL points at the mutable `refs/heads/main` of a personal GitHub repository owned by the same author, so the content fed into the author-controlled parser can change at any time after publish. The combination of a hollow package, a lookalike build/runtime dependency, and install-time fetching of unpinned content from a personal GitHub branch into an author-controlled parser is a dropper-lure shape: installing extrahtml resolves and executes attacker-controlled code on the installer's host, with no legitimate functionality shipped by the package itself.

In this campaign, remote code is executed via a dependency pretending to be a YAML loader but embedding a special loader executing code from a provided file. During analysis, the code was just a stub.

Category: MALICIOUS - The campaign has clearly malicious intent, like infostealers.

Campaign: 2026-11-parseyaml

Reasons (based on the campaign):

 - The malicious code is intentionally included in a dependency of the package

 - Downloads and executes a remote malicious script.

setup.py performs an unconditional HTTP GET at install time to the hardcoded bare IP http://38.242.235.206/depconf/doctreelstm/setup-py, sending the installer's username (USER/USERNAME env), hostname (socket.gethostname()), and current working directory as query parameters. The destination is a cleartext bare-IP endpoint, not a first-party registry or vendor host, and the beacon fires on `pip install` with no documentation, no opt-out, and no caller configuration. The package ships no functional code and self-describes as a defensive placeholder squatting an internal project name, but that framing is author-controlled and does not change that installer identity + host + cwd leave the machine to an attacker-controlled destination on install.

Installing the package or importing the module exfiltrates basic information about the host, and the package has no other purpose.
